learningObjective: Distinguish `torch.cond` from `torch.where` and identify when each is the appropriate rewrite for a data-dependent branch.

canonicalClaims.claim: `torch.where(cond, a, b)` evaluates both arms and selects per element; `torch.cond(cond, fn_true, fn_false, operands)` captures each arm as a subgraph and only one arm runs at execution time. Both are compile-friendly (Inductor lowers `torch.where` to pointwise select; `torch.cond` is preserved as a control-flow op through torch.export).
nonImplications: Does not imply one is universally faster; the trade-off depends on arm cost.
Does not imply torch.cond avoids all guards / specialization.

misconceptions.claim: torch.where is semantically incorrect for data-dependent selection.
misconceptions.whyWrong: torch.where selects per element with a well-defined semantics; it is a valid rewrite when both arms are cheap.

misconceptions.claim: torch.cond is deprecated in favor of torch.where.
misconceptions.whyWrong: torch.cond is a current API for control-flow capture.

misconceptions.claim: torch.where captures each arm as a subgraph and only one runs.
misconceptions.whyWrong: torch.where evaluates both arms; only torch.cond captures separate subgraphs.

implementationFacts: torch.where lowers to pointwise select in Inductor
torch.cond captures each arm as an FX subgraph
torch.cond is preserved through torch.export (as a HigherOrderOp)
performanceScenarios: For very cheap arms, torch.where is often faster (fully parallel); for expensive/asymmetric arms, torch.cond avoids wasted work.
